newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - Poland aims at tight budget for election year.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Poland aims at tight budget for election year.

text.p: Poland can maintain a balance between healthy growth and fiscal discipline in 1997 even though analysts see little room for bold reforms and deficit-slashing in the year of general elections.
The ruling leftist coalition has already agreed a 1997 budget outline which assumes a deficit of 2.6 percent of gross domestic product, down from this year's planned 2.8 percent.

Poland aims to join the European Union this century and the budget shortfall would be roughly in line with the EU Maastricht treaty criteria for monetary union of a ceiling of three percent, even when the overall public sector deficit, which includes local governments budgets, is taken into account.
The budget would also ensure that the public debt/GDP ratio stays below the 60-percent ceiling set in Maastricht.
BUDGET LESS TIGHT THAN EXPECTED AS ELECTIONS LOOM
Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko has said he aims to reduce year-on-year inflation to 13 percent in 1997 from this year's target of 17 percent, while securing 5.5 percent growth.

The 1997 deficit reduction is smaller than earlier envisaged but analysts say Kolodko will still have to fight hard to defend it as the parliamentary elections, due late in 1997, make it tempting for the ruling coalition to boost spending.

"I think we will see a lack of consistency within the coalition with some ministers trying to maintain discipline while others push for vote-winning handouts," said Janusz Dabrowski, of the independent Gdansk Market Economy Institute.
The debate is expected to start later this month with the final finance ministry draft due this week and the government obliged to submit its bill to parliament by the end of October.
The parliament then has three months to pass the law and faces dissolution if it fails to meet the deadline.
CAPPING PENSION GROWTH IS KEY TEST OF CREDIBILITY
Analysts say one key issue will be whether a government plan to cap pensions growth at only 2.5 percent above inflation survives parliamentary debates.

"As in the past (achieving the planned deficit) will require...moderation in expenditure...especially in the area of social transfers," said Markus Rodlauer, the International Monetary Fund's Warsaw representative.
"It is vital that the government's current proposal for pension indexation in 1997 materialises," he said.
He added that the government should aim for as low a deficit as possible and leave some margin for manoeuvre.
LEFT-WING GOVERNMENT HAS RECORD OF MAINTAINING DISCIPLINE

Analysts say the coalition of the ex-communist social democrats and the smaller Polish Peasant Party might find it politically desirable to boost spending on benefits for the country's nine million pensioners ahead of the vote.
But they also point to Kolodko' strong track record on maintaining fiscal discipline and do not foresee any radical loosening of budget restraints.

"The next 12 months will not be most suitable for reforming the economy but...there have already been several occasions when the leftist government could have been tempted to loosen up and did not," said Tomasz Jedrzejczak, investment analyst at Bank Handlowy SA securities unit.

Analysts also say the government's decision on Tuesday to keep personal income taxes unchanged, despite an earlier pledge to cut them next year, although unpopular, would help offset additional pressures for more spending.
"In the longer-term it would be desirable to gradually lower taxes but I will feel more comfortable if taxes stay unchanged next year," one analyst said.
INFLATION REMAINS A CHALLENGE, BUT GENERAL OUTLOOK POSITIVE

Analysts say inflation is likely to be the biggest challenge and, ironically, a possible success in bringing price growth this year close to the 17 percent target could make meeting the 1997 target harder by creating pent-up pressure.

They say this year's likely dip in inflation from 21.6 percent in 1995 would largely be achieved because of slower than planned rises of official prices of energy and a delay in the planned liberalisation of fuel prices.
But pressures from high world oil prices and demands of higher coal prices may prove too strong to resist.
"The government is sacrificing a long-term goal of keeping a steady downward inflation path for a short-term target of meeting the 1996 goal, and we may have a rebound early in 1997," Dabrowski said.

Analysts stress Poland will tackle next year's challenges from a very comfortable position with the economy likely to grow by 5-6 percent on strong domestic demand and Western recovery and almost $18 billion in foreign exchange reserves.

But many are sceptical whether the ruling coalition will risk pushing ahead next year with a long overdue reform of the social security system and a speeding up of privatisation -- both seen as crucial to sustaining long-term growth.
